state: People often assume that having more choices gives them greater freedom and satisfaction. However, an excessive number of options can make decision-making more difficult. When consumers are faced with dozens of similar products, they may spend more time comparing minor differences and become less confident about their final decision. In some cases, they may even avoid making a choice altogether. Thus, while choice is generally valuable, increasing the number of available options does not always improve the experience of choosing.

state: Scientific progress often depends not only on discovering new facts but also on questioning ideas that have long been accepted. Established theories provide useful frameworks for understanding the world, yet they can also limit the way researchers interpret unexpected evidence. A scientist who treats an existing theory as unquestionable may ignore observations that do not fit it. By contrast, researchers who remain willing to revise their assumptions are more likely to recognize patterns that others overlook.
